Mr. Speaker, last Thursday in the debate on government motion No. 2 on language rights in Canada, I was denied the opportunity to participate. Since I was not recognized, the question was put to the House. Other members missed the opportunity to debate as well. In other words, the debate collapsed.
If you look at Hansard, page 8414, you will find the following:
Is the House ready for the question?
No.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sorry but I cannot recognize the hon. member.
He is not properly dressed.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the motion was subsequently carried without further debate.
My question of privilege today is the fact that I was not recognized for such debate. Might I add that my question of privilege is rooted on one basic question: Is our parliamentary institution well served when dress is more important than debate? In other words, is a tie more important than a message?
Mr. Speaker, under your leadership we have made great progress one step at a time. A balance has been struck between the individual rights of members in this Chamber and collective rights of the House so as to make this institution function and cany out the nation's business. We all appreciate that fact.
In the realm of individual rights, women in this Chamber can dress in a variety of ways according to
fashion and changing trends. I am glad of that fact and support it. The question now is whether the same flexibility can be extended for men as well. In making the case for modernizing the dress code for male members, may I quote the Deputy Speaker from page 6908 of Hansard of December 14, 1989, when he said:
I think most members are aware of the way members should dress in the House. It is stated quite clearly in Beauchesne's that the dress of members should be conservative, contemporary dress. That is the rule.
He added:
It does happen, when we have votes, that members may come in at the last second and may not technically fit the criteria set out in Beauchesne's. It is for that reason that in the past we have allowed those members their voting privileges. However, if the time came for the member to speak in the House then the decision of the Chair could be different.
Clearly the Deputy Speaker with his ruling left the door wide open, I submit. You will also find that last Thursday, at page 8399 of Hansard, the government house leader stated that debate on government motion No. 2 would continue for several days. Because of his assurance several members of the House, myself included, were taken rather by surprise when no member in the customary round of speakers rose to continue debate following the conclusion of the first round.
Therefore, at the last second I had to rise in order for debate to continue. My situation was therefore comparable to the one the Deputy Speaker described last December. Might I stress, Mr. Speaker, before concluding, that the only rule of the House that refers to members appearance is Standing Order 17. It states:
Every member desiring to speak is to rise in his or her place, uncovered, and address the Speaker.
I conformed with such rule last Thursday. While it is true Beauschene's is often quoted in the matter of member's dress, I think it is important to remember that Beauchesne is an interpretation of the rules, not the rule itself. The rules of the House are set out in the Standing Orders and I fully complied with Standing Order 17.

February 19, 1990
Private Members' Business
To bring this Chamber into the 20th century you may want to address this question today: what is more important, jacket and tie or message and debate? Would you consider therefore, Mr. Speaker, referring this matter to the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure while at the same time providing us with your ruling for our guidance until the committee has reported?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

The hon. member has raised a matter which has been raised in this chamber a number of times before. The hon. member is an experienced member and he puts the point with a certain eloquence.
I am of course concerned that the complaint that is brought in front of us is that, because of his dress, the hon. member was not able to enter into a debate which was at that moment about to collapse. It may well be that hon. members will want to change our present practices but I must be cognizant of what they are. speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of expanding literacy programs in federal penitentiaries.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to ask the House to endorse the motion I placed on the Order Paper calling on the government to consider the advisability of expanding literacy programs in federal penitentiaries.
This of course is International Literacy Year and I am rising to ask the House to address itself to a particular aspect of the problem of illiteracy in Canada, the quality of our programs in Canada's federal prisons.
We in Parliament have a special responsibility for the level of programming in Canadian prisons. We have no excuses in this House if the job is not properly done. We cannot blame the provinces, school boards, colleges, universities, municipal governments or the general community. We have only ourselves to hold responsible for the fact that our programs are not adequate.
It is important at the outset of Literacy Year that we in this House call on the Correctional Service of Canada, the Solicitor General and the government to address this and that we in this House focus our attention on this particularly sensitive and difficult problem.
Let me say at the outset that I acknowledge the Correctional Service of Canada is working at the problem. It has had in place for some time a literacy initiative program. The issue is whether the program is satisfactory and sufficient to deal with the problem. I hope that members of the government will rise today and tell us in detail and in specific terms that that is exactly what is happening. The information I have indicates that the programs are lacking, and this is expressed in statistics and in human suffering. A survey in 1989 demonstrated that 65 per cent of our prison population is functionally illiterate. This means that 65 per cent of the people in our prisons Cannot read simple instructions on a cough syrup bottle, cannot fill out simple forms, cannot understand sections of the Charter of Rights, or pick out correct numbers from a list or page of numbers. In the general population, there are in the area of 22 per cent to 24 per cent who are functionally illiterate. That in itself is a scandal in this country, but 65 per cent of our prison population is currently illiterate and we must do something about it.
The federal government program presently in place is called the Adult Basic Education Program. This program is, to the extent that it is in place, attempting to come to grips with the problem. I want to pay particular tribute to the previous Solicitor General, Mr. Kelleher, who actually convened a national conference in 1987 on offender literacy. Unfortunately, the current administration appears not to be following up on the concern and initiative shown by the previous Solicitor General. I may add that even that Solicitor General neglected to invite
February 19, 1990

those most directly concerned with the program, the prisoners and ex-prisoners.
In 1989, a special study funded by the Secretary of State was undertaken by the John Howard Society. The researcher involved with the society was Kimberley Pate and her report was filed in August, 1989. This report reviews thoroughly the adequacy of the literacy programs in our prisons and I rely heavily on that for the comments and criticisms that I have.
In addition, as critic for the Solicitor General for the New Democratic Party, I have received probably a thousand letters from prisoners in our institutions. The recurring theme in these letters is the inadequacy of the programs in prisons. I hope this debate will focus some attention on the problem and perhaps start some action on it.
The first problem is that the program is compulsory. Prisoners are forced to take it if, after a test, they are demonstrated to be "functionally illiterate". The compulsory element of the Correctional Service of Canada program was trashed by the conference in 1987, yet it continues to this day. The element of compulsion flies in the face of every pedagogical understanding currently at hand. It simply does not and cannot work. The John Howard Society report of 1989 confirms that.
Let me refer the House to some of the comments made by inmates who were interviewed in that study. One said:
It is really stupid, you know. They (the CSC policy developers and program ministers) cannot really believe the old saying about how you can take a horse to water and it will finally drink once it gets thirsty. Forcing people who are already embarrassed and have been taught to keep all your weaknesses hidden in places like this, in jail, to then sit in the beginning classes where everyone can see you are dummy-man, that is just plain stupid. The only reason most of us say we want to learn stuff is to play the game and get out. We waste everyone else's time, for them who really want to learn. Know what I mean? Maybe if they stop forcing the issue we might really go on our own.
The second problem is that in developing the program there was no consultation with the users of the program. It is hard to imagine, but it is true. There was no discussion with prisoners or inmates about the nature of
Private Members' Business
the program. There is no ongoing effort to evaluate with them what kind of program should be undertaken.
Third, the program resources have been stolen from other educational programs, contrary to the clear commitment of the Solicitor General at the time the program was instituted. Instead of taking the program from research, travel, consultants, where they said they would, they have taken it from the other educational programs in the institutions.
That reduces those programs to a new level of inadequacy and removes the incentive for proceeding into the higher levels that really count in the final analysis, getting a job once the inmates are out.
Another problem is that the testing on this program is completely inadequate. The test program was developed over 20 years ago in California. It is denounced in every review of the literacy program, and as I understand it, the Correctional Service of Canada has already conceded that the testing program is inadequate. I want to hear today that there in fact has been a change.
Although it is an unwritten rule, there are targets or quotas established for the institutions in order that the Correctional Service of Canada can look good when asked questions in Parliament about this program. There are a number of problems with those targets. First, they are easy to manipulate. Even more important and more significant is that the targets encourage the staff to work with the students who are up to a grade 6 to grade 8 level. That means they are ignoring the students at the lower levels, the students who most require the kind of help that an effective literacy program can be.
Let me refer again to the Pate study, page 16:
If this is indeed the case then the ironic result of the CSC ABE
initiative may be that proportionately less time may now be being
devoted to working with this group than was the case prior to
Kelleher's program announcement in 1987.
The tutoring, according to the study, is inadequate and is not trusted by the participants.
The program is simply not reaching the targeted prison population. At least half of the prison population who need the program are not taking any program at all, notwithstanding the compulsory nature.
Finally, there is no follow-up. Once the prisoners leave prison no facility is provided through the Correctional Service program in which they can maintain,

February 19, 1990
Private Members' Business
increase and improve any progress they have made while they were on the inside.
This is a program that is improperly and inadequately funded, has not been thought through, that is developed without consultation with the people who are taking the program. The tutoring and teaching is below standard. There is no follow-up, and the very foundation of the program undercuts its effectiveness. This is taking place in a section of our population where the pay-offs for an effective literacy program would be most significant.
What do we do about it, Mr. Speaker?
First, there is client involvement. Obviously there has to be some thorough discussion with inmates in developing the program.
Second, we have to end the mandatory requirement.
Third, there should be the provision of financial incentives to take the program.
Fourth, community and volunteer teaching needs to be written into the program so that there is seen within the institution to be some level of independence by the teachers. As well, it can form part of a program of increasing the ability to relate to those who are on the outside and in the general community.
Fifth, we have to improve the peer tutoring that has apparently shown some positive signs. It has also shown some negatives. Those negatives need to be addressed.
Sixth, there has to be an improved information network across Canada to know what is working and what is not working.
Seventh, and perhaps most important, there must be an integration of the literacy programs with other life skills programs in our prisons. It has to be part of a package that will assist those who need the benefits that a good literacy program can bring. It has been said that literacy has a certain political attractiveness. It is easy for a minister to institute such a program in that area.
We need to focus on genuine life skills and the literacy program needs to be seen as part of that. That may also
help to undercut some of the stereotypes within the prison that seem to be undercutting the program.
Eight, there must be some effective follow-up with some programs designed for that purpose.
With those remarks, Mr. Speaker, I ask the House to give positive consideration to this motion. I appreciate that under the practice of this House, it is not likely today to come to a vote, but I hope it will have the support of members. I hope the Correctional Service of Canada is listening and that the Solicitor General will give his undertaking to this House that there will be in this literacy year some very specific personal attention from him to this important program in Canada's prisons.
Let me conclude by putting this in the larger context, and if I may be permitted a mild partisan note, to put on record the position of the New Democratic Party at its most recent convention in Winnipeg on the issue of literacy. At that convention the New Democratic Party adopted the following resolution:
That the New Democratic Party supports the development and implementation of policies to ensure every adult full access to and participation in adult literacy programs which would be developed in co-operation with the provinces, the literacy community and the trade union movement. Such policies would:
1.	include all the necessary types of funding mechanisms at levels adequate to allow adults to exercise their right to participate in free adult basic education;
2.	assume the involvement of large numbers of literacy workers in recognition of the fact that the volunteer sector cannot meet all the needs of illiterate adults;
3.	recognize the need for a range of programming options including community-based programs and on-the-job programs sponsored by trade unions which respond to the needs of individuals and groups;
4.	assume the provision of adequate facilities, relevant learning materials and related services such as child care, transportation and counselling;
5.	be part of a larger policy initiative to attack the economic and social conditions which contribute to the continued existence of adult illiteracy;
6.	direct funding to Indian and Northern Affairs to improve basic education on reserves and ensure access to a grade 12 education on reserves; and
7.	expand literacy programs in federal penitentiaries.
I commend this program and the resolution to the House and I ask for your support.
February 19, 1990

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FEDERAL PENITENTIARIES LITERACY PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us is to consider expanding literacy programs in federal penitentiaries. The federal government and Correctional Service Canada support this motion, as do I. The federal government and the CSC have already taken measures required to deal with the problems posed by illiteracy among inmates in federal penitentiaries.
The dignity of the individual, the rights of all members of society, the potential for personal growth, and the development of human beings are essential considerations in the effort to help offenders to become law-abiding citizens. The CSC initiative is in response to the Throne Speech of October, 1986, in which the federal government committed itself to co-operating with the provinces, the private sector and voluntary organizations in developing ways to allow Canadians to acquire the degree of literacy required to take full advantage of the benefits of an advanced society.
Following a series of visits to several penitentiaries, the then Solicitor General assessed the extent of the problem and decided to tackle the problem head on. The Solicitor General declared that improving basic adult education programs was a priority for Correctional Service Canada. As a result, the CSC launched a three-year program to reduce functional illiteracy among federal inmates by 5 per cent annually between April 1, 1987, and March 31, 1989.
It is important to note that my hon. friend criticized the program because there were quotas imposed. There has to be an objective in place. The CSC used the definition of functional illiteracy adopted by UNESCO, and that is the equivalent of a grade eight education. Because of the various educational systems that exist in Canada, the CSC uses the completion of grade eight in language and mathematics as a standard for purposes of comparison.
According to the mission statement of the CSC, Correctional Service Canada, as part of the criminal justice system contributes to the protection of society by actively encouraging and assisting offenders to become law-abiding citizens while exercising reasonable, safe, secure and humane control.
The CSC knows how illiteracy affects inmates. An inmate who can neither read nor write is ill equipped to face the demands of everyday life or to find a job. Even
Private Members' Business
though it has not yet been possible to establish a direct correlation between illiteracy and recidivism, the correlation between unemployment and a lack of basic education and technical skills cannot be disputed.
According to Statistics Canada unemployment is highest among those with less than a grade eight education. Standardized tests have also shown that the illiteracy rate among inmates is more than twice that of the general Canadian population. When considering the many factors that contribute to crime, we must recognize that illiterate people have fewer options, less choice and greater difficulty in improving their lives than those who can read and write.
In practice only 150 inmates were able to complete grade eight in 1986-87. It was decided at that time that the objective for 1987-88 would be to have five times as many inmates complete the basic adult education program, for a grand total of 750. The objective for 1988-89 would be 1,200 more inmates, and for 1989-90, 1,800 more. The over-all objective of CSC was therefore to have in excess of 4,050 inmates complete at least a grade eight education during this three-year period. I think my hon. friend will have to admit that that is a very worth-while objective.
This ambitious initiative was intended to demonstrate the firm commitment of CSC to combating illiteracy among inmates. It is vital that people understand that the vast majority of inmates incarcerated in our penitentiaries will be released some day. They will be released on parole, under mandatory supervision, or simply because they have completed their sentence. To be a capable member of society they must have an improved education.
The National Parole Board takes the inmate's participation in the basic education program into account before making a decision on parole. My hon. friend talks about incentives. I think that would be incentive enough to get people to take this program. Perhaps more than anything else this makes inmates understand how important the ability to read and write is in being able to function properly in the outside world.
In 1988 the average inmate, or 57 per cent of the prison population, was serving a sentence of less than six years. During the first year of this initiative, that is during the 1987-88 fiscal year, 1,042 inmates or 139 per cent of the objective completed grade eight. In 1988-89,

Private Members' Business
1,446 more inmates completed grade eight, with the objective being 1,200.
During the first two years of this initiative the CSC has achieved 118 per cent of its objective. The third year appears to have started well since roughly 80 per cent of the over-all objective had been obtained by the end of the second quarter. The CSC certainly hopes to be able to meet its over-all objective.
To achieve this end, the CSC budgeted 100 per cent more in 1987-88 than in 1986-87 for basic adult education, an increase from $2.5 million to $5 million. In 1988-89 the over-all budget for adult basic education was roughly $6.4 million. I should stress that the CSC maintained all the other educational programs it offers to federal inmates including secondary, post-secondary and college education programs. Vocational training also continues to be a crucial component of the program offered since it allows inmates to learn a craft or skill directly.
The service has also established standard mandatory testing to identify functionally illiterate offenders and thus be better able to integrate them into the adult basic education program. Since commencement of the initiative close to 8,000 inmates entering the correctional system have undergone testing. To date, about 65 per cent have scored at lower than the completed grade eight level. The rate of refusal-and I think it is important to say "refusal" because my hon. friend said that this program was mandatory-to undergo testing has decreased from 16 per cent to 8 per cent in two years. The tests used are currently under revision in order to improve further the service's effectiveness at identifying illiterate inmates.
During the course of 1988-89 the correctional service set up a new system to manage data on inmate education, thus enabling the service to monitor the fulfilment of its objectives even more closely. For example, it was noted, with the help of this new system, that the average national success rate in relation to the number of inmates registered dropped from 2.99 in March of 1988 to 2.59 in April of 1989, a significant drop.
This demonstrates better case management and more careful follow-up of students who withdraw or fail. In fact the service has set in motion an entire process aimed
at assisting these students with problems and encouraging them to return to the program by modifying for them the traditional approach to teaching. The cost per successful case has decreased from $4,650 in 1987-88 to $4,189 in 1988-89. This accomplishment greatly surpasses the initial objective of $5,000 per case.
Correctional Service Canada now uses innovative teaching methods to help inmates surmount perceptual problems and identified learning disabilities. The service has expanded the adult basic education program and will continue to make improvements to increase participation and effectiveness. Also, inmate involvement in this program must henceforth be taken into account when considering the inmate for certain jobs in the institution. In some cases the inmate's participation is a condition for obtaining special privileges within the institution.
Training sessions on learning disabilities have been offered to teaching staff in order to improve their ability to assist inmates with these problems. All staff have been made aware of the importance of basic education in order that a concerted movement be established throughout the correctional service to combat the problem of illiteracy.
In addition to ensuring that adult basic education programs are accredited, the service has adopted a multitude of techniques and methods aimed at facilitating adult learning. These include small group or individual instruction if necessary, computer assisted teaching, the use of tutors from within the prison population, as well as more effective use of community volunteers. My hon. friend spoke about the use of peers and community volunteers, integration with other life skills programs and follow-up. I want to point out to my hon. friend that these are all things that are being done. In fact training programs have been given to these volunteers in some regions.
Adult basic education does much more than teach people the three r's. It provides offenders with the opportunity to feel better about themselves and experience personal growth, which will assist them when they are released. As with the general public, however, education of offenders does not end with grade eight completion. On the contrary, offenders who successfully complete the adult education program are encouraged to
February 19, 1990

continue with their studies in secondary, college level and post-secondary education.
To emphasize the importance that education plays in everyone's life, a communications strategy will be developed that explains to all offenders the importance of education to their successful reintegration into society.
Literacy programs already in place in our federal penitentiaries have turned out to be very successful. CSC is working to co-operate with the provinces to maintain course quality and to obtain provincial accreditation. It must be understood that inmate literacy should lead to job training or a pursuit of higher levels of education.
In this regard the CSC also plans, in coming years, to emphasize inmate participation in obtaining a grade ten education while continuing to promote the achievement of grade eight as a priority. In addition, the service will establish a global strategy of surmounting the learning disabilities of inmates.
In conclusion, I therefore believe that the federal government, through the intervention of CSC, is promoting the social reintegration of inmates through adult basic education. The results are a clear indication of the efforts that have been made in this area. I can assure you that the correctional service will continue its work in this regard.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FEDERAL PENITENTIARIES LITERACY PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to support the motion proposed by my hon. colleague. I would initially like to review the problem of literacy quickly.
Many will recall that literacy has been noted by Southam and a number of other researchers to affect roughly 25 per cent of Canadians. We are told that there are approximately five million functionally illiterate Canadians today. It is important to spend a few seconds on what is meant by functional illiteracy. It means that a person is unable to read, write or compute at a level satisfactory to be able to give all himself or herself to society or to take away from society, from his or her community, as much as he or she would if the literacy rate were higher than it is now.
As I indicated we have roughly five million functionally illiterate people in Canada. They come from a variety of groups. For example, there are older Canadians who are involved in a disproportionate number because they
Private Members' Business
did not have the same kinds of opportunities that we had. They were needed to go to work earlier than we were.
There are also aboriginal people who have not had the same opportunities as other Canadians, and of course that situation is being corrected rather rapidly.
There are new Canadians, some of them already literate in a language other than English or French and some of them who need special assistance in this area.
There are people with learning difficulties and learning handicaps. There are also Canadians who at one time in their lives were functionally literate, but because society has changed so rapidly and there are more demands being made in the field of reading, writing and computing, they are no longer considered functionally literate. However, today we are talking specifically about our inmate population.
I want to say a few words about this particular population. According to certain media reports there are roughly 12,000 people in our federal penitentiaries, and the rates of illiteracy vary according to the source. I have read that it is from 40 per cent up to 75 per cent. I have heard today 65 per cent. In other documentation I have seen 50 per cent. I think we could agree that it is a high rate, higher than the national average, and clearly we need to do something special about it.
I have also been told by these same sources that only 500 people a year were participating in literacy programs a few years ago and perhaps 150 of those 500 had completed the programs. Those numbers have improved during the last few years, but there is still a lot of room to move.
Let me quote from a special report about literacy entitled "Breaking Down Invisible Walls":
In a society where non-readers are on the fringes, unable to
participate fully, literacy training can go a long way in keeping
ex-inmates out of prison.
We have to realize that literacy is one thing that can contribute to rehabilitation. It cannot do it all, but clearly it can contribute.
Literacy is not only reading, writing and computing. Those are important by themselves obviously in a society such as ours, one which is changing remarkably quickly and where those demands are in fact increasing on a daily basis, but we are also talking about life skills:

February 19, 1990
Private Members' Business
learning how to live out of the penitentiary environment, learning how to live within the whole of society.
We are also talking about restoration of self-respect. Without that restoration of self-respect there can be little gain made in this area. There can be little hope to reintegrate successfully in society. We have to remember as well that literacy for people who are incarcerated is a toe-hold for further education and training. It is absolutely critical to have a certain degree of literacy in order to be able to profit fully from it.
Some will know that the correctional service is organized into seven major categories. I want to quote one section because I think it is particularly relevant. It is the section entitled "Education, Training and Employment of Inmates". It reads as follows:
To maximize employment, training and educational opportunities for all offenders in preparation for their reintegration into society as productive citizens. This is achieved by increasing the Correctional Service's capacity to provide meaningful work and training opportunities; by increasing, where appropriate, the emphasis on work programs that will generate revenue to help offset the operating cost of their Service; and by effectively supporting the efforts of released inmates to find gainful employment.
We have here one particular sector devoted almost entirely to ensuring that our inmates are given those kinds of opportunities educationally and in related fields to ensuring that they can integrate fully into Canadian society. The emphasis placed on literacy is one of critical importance.

I will give a brief summary in French. As I said earlier, there are roughly 12,000 inmates in our federal penitentiaries. A few years ago, only 500 inmates were involved and perhaps 1'50 actually completed literacy programs. Those figures are much higher today, but we still have a long way to go. We have to realize that literacy is not only reading, writing, and arithmetic. We are also talking about developing self-respect and learning how to live outside the penitentiaiy.

I believe that we need to do everything as a society to ensure that inmates do not return to prison. Thousands of dollars-there are large figures which indicate in excess of $50,000 per year to keep someone incarcerated-are in fact being spent with increasing frequency. I
would suggest that we need to invest in literacy and other related programs.
My colleague has documented rather well some of the inadequacies of the program. Let me briefly repeat those that I support. It is compulsory, and this is causing certain difficulty. Surely there are ways to bring about greater participation rates without mandating it. We need to have programs that are brought forward in consultation with particular individuals involved in a significant kind of way. We need to ensure that the learning materials are the most appropriate. We need to make certain that the test programs are the most adequate possible.
The targets may in fact be inappropriate. We need to review that as well. It is important to recognize that one of the effective ways is through tutoring. We recognize as well that tutoring has not always been as successful as it might have been. Perhaps the greatest inadequacy has been in the follow-up, what happens after the individual leaves the penitentiary.
We must first respond to the criticisms that have been made. We just cannot take them lightly. They are valid criticisms and there are ways of counteracting them.
There are incentives that could be brought forward, monetary and other. We need to explore that and see what might be done in order to get larger participation rates. We need to improve our methods of instruction, and we need to look very closely at tutoring and how it can be improved to make a greater contribution. As I indicated before we definitely need to ensure that the follow-ups are adequate.

Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I want to ask the government to ensure that the necessary funding is provided so that our inmates can take full advantage of these literacy and education programs and be intergrated into Canadian society.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FEDERAL PENITENTIARIES LITERACY PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the motion of the hon. member for Victoria. The Secretary of State has stated that the Government of Canada has two goals for this year, which is International Literacy Year. The first is to prevent
February 19, 1990

illiteracy; the second is to help those who have fallen through the cracks.
Today I want to talk about one group that has fallen through those cracks, and those are people who are currently residing in federal penitentiaries. In 1981 nearly 40 per cent of inmates of federal penitentiaries had less than a grade nine education, nearly 10 per cent higher than the general population of Canada. Only 2 per cent of those who need to improve their literacy skills are currently enrolled in programs.
We need to reach out to those people and find ways to make them want to enrol in literacy programs. The inmates of our federal penitentiaries should receive no less than what we wish for others in our society, especially where literacy programs are concerned.
There needs to be provision of literacy services which are flexible enough to fit the individual's need. They should also have policies to take into account the diversity of the background of the individual and his or her learning experiences prior to being incarcerated.
However I agree with previous speakers that they must be voluntary programs. No one should be forced to participate in a literacy program because they happen to be behind bars. It must be the individual's choice, but it must be available and not only while the inmate is in prison. If the course is not completed when the inmate leaves prison, he or she must be able to continue it.
The causes of literacy are many, but the majority of learners had negative experience with formal education and require a comfortable learning environment. Literacy programs must be creative, must be interesting, and must meet the needs of those who in fact dropped out of school because the programs failed them.
All human beings, according to the UNESCO international conference on adult education in 1985, have the right to learn and read and write in their native language. It is an objective to which Canada should be aspiring.
In September 1988 the Prime Minister said: "We are placing literacy high on the national agenda. We want one Canada united, prosperous, with equal opportunities for all of our citizens."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to take part in this debate. Clearly members on all sides of the House veiy much support its intent. As my colleague, the member for Mississauga West mentioned earlier, the federal government, the Correctional Service of Canada and the Solicitor General very much support this motion.
Correctional Service Canada has already taken the necessary measures. The adult basic education program this department offers has been a priority since 1987, and the program has had considerable success. Since this initiative was begun, 3,200 inmates have completed grade eight courses in language and mathematics.
Before making one or two other comments I want to say that I had an opportunity many years ago while working as a chaplain in several prisons to realize the direct relationship between illiteracy and crime. It perhaps is stating something that is obvious to those who have had anything to do with our criminal justice system, but there is a very high correlation between people who have had an inadequate or non-existent education and those who get in trouble with the law. It seems to me to be abundantly obvious. I am sorry it has taken us so long to begin the sensible programs that are very much needed while people are incarcerated to ensure that they have the opportunity to make a different life for themselves when they are finally released.
This year, 1990, has been declared International Literacy Year by the United Nations General Assembly. To celebrate International Literacy Year, Correctional Service Canada will launch a book voyage in conjunction with the project of the International Task Force on Literacy. The idea is to get learners involved in International Literacy Year.

February 19, 1990
A committee will travel from institution to institution collecting stories, poems and other forms of written expression which adult basic education students have written. Other similar books are being prepared around the world. At the end of the year, a giant book with selections from all those submitted will be translated into other major languages and will be presented by the International Committee of Learners to the Secretary General of the United Nations at a ceremony at the UN headquarters on December 10, this year.
Another way in which Correctional Service Canada will celebrate this year is to co-host an international conference, entitled "Freedom to Read", an international conference on literacy and corrections with the United States Department of the Attorney General. Delegates representing nations from around the world will be invited to participate in the conference scheduled for October 15 to October 17, 1990, providing an opportunity for correctional educational professionals and administrators to share ideas and experience regarding methods, standards and services related to literacy and offenders.
I believe this kind of initiative speaks well not only for the Government of Canada but certainly for this Parliament which has clearly demonstrated in these past few minutes, with the initiative of the member for Victoria, how important it is to get at the underlying causes of criminal activity and continuing criminal activity in Canada. I welcome and support it veiy much.

Mr. Speaker, I understand that Mr. Bob White was in Canso and had the Leader of the New Democratic Party in tow with him for a public demonstration indicating the attention of the CLC and the New Democratic Party to a problem that has been of deep concern to this government since it arose.
Oral Questions
The hon. member will understand that a demonstration is not going to solve this problem and that we have very serious problems in the Atlantic fishery.
It is not simply Canso that is affected. It is Lockeport and a number of other communities in Newfoundland and in Nova Scotia that are very directly affected by this problem. We are seeking to find solutions that will be durable solutions.
Some of these issues, as the hon. leader will learn if she stays longer in her job, require more than a demonstration to resolve them.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
If this government and its members cared about the people of Atlantic Canada, if they cared about the community of Canso, they would have been standing at that meeting in Canso telling the people of Canso their solutions.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, on February 11 a fisheries official indicated that community-based quotas are being considered by the federal government.
Principle three of the 1990 Atlantic Groundfish Management Plan states that allocation of fishery resources will be on the basis of equity, taking into account closeness to the resource, and the relative dependence of coastal communities upon a given resource.
Will the minister listen to the supporters of Canso and the Atlantic communities? Will he commit himself today to bring forward community-based quotas?
Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): Mr. Speaker, the official quoted was responding, I think, at a special seminar organized by the Maritime Fishermen's Union, to a question about community quotas among a variety of options for dealing with this problem.
I believe it was the ADM for the Atlantic region who indicated that if this option were to be considered, a number of factors should be taken into account. He explained why community quotas lead to a less econom-

February 19, 1990
Oral Questions
ic, less competitive fishery and more hardship and suffering for all those who rely on this industry because, in fact, plants are operated at very low levels of their optimal capacity.
We have to look at such proposals in the context of our historical policy which is not to allocate specific quantities of fish to specific communities.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the minister.
It is this government's responsibility to represent the people and not National Sea.
Shameless waste of perfectly edible fish has gone on for years. It is thrown back in the sea. Our resources and our environment must be treated with respect.
Mr. Speaker, this scandalous waste must stop. Can the minister guarantee that starting today every fish caught will be used?
Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): Mr. Speaker, the federal government represents all the people in the Atlantic region and not only those who have interests-

On the question of fish that are wasted at sea, this is a despicable practice. In some cases in the fishery there is an unavoidable by-catch of undersized fish because fish are caught with nets and fish tend to gather up in nets.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
I think all members of the House recognize that fact, Mr. Speaker.
We take every measure management-wise to minimize the waste of fish by all sectors of the industry. In regard to the offshore sector, it is recognized that this practice does occur and that is why we have observers on these vessels to minimize and prevent these kinds of wasteful practices.

Mr. Speaker, the long awaited Harris report on the northern cod stock was delivered to the Minister of Fisheries today. According to the scientific evidence and the testimony given by experienced fishermen before the Harris panel, today the northern cod stock is involved in
that very delicate pre-spawning activity that is so vital for the actual spawning itself.
Will the Government of Canada now take the advice of these experienced fishermen and cancel the licences of every foreign trawler licensed by this government inside of our 200-mile zone for 1990, foreign trawlers that outnumber the Canadian offshore fleet two to one, trawlers that are three and four times the size of our Canadian boats?
Can the minister assure us that he will put an end to this foreign disruption of the pre-spawning process of the northern cod stock and cancel every licence?
Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows that when foreign vessels fish inside the 200-mile economic zone, it is because Canada is obliged to make surplus stocks available to the vessels of other countries that belong to the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization outside the 12-mile limit.
Those stocks do not belong to Canada, although we are given first opportunity to use them for the benefit of our fishermen and communities such as Canso. That is why we have made 100,000 tonnes of those surplus stocks available to our own fishermen on a priority basis.
Scientists advise me there is no recorded evidence in the scientific literature or our own research which states that fishing on the spawning grounds does measurable damage to the cod stocks. I have had private confirmation of that from Dr. Harris. We will be doing additional research on this question, but I should point out that where fisheries have been conducted in the North Sea and in Canadian waters in the 1960s, on the spawning stocks, we have seen abundant production from those resources in subsequent years.
So this question can in no way be answered in a simplistic fashion as this member is often wont to do.

Mr. Speaker, two weeks ago in the House the minister told us that the food of the cod fish that is being given to the foreigners is under-utilized species, that food has nothing to do with the weight of the codfish.
Today he is telling us that according to his advice the disruption of the spawning ground has nothing to do with the spawning process. He must be getting his advice from a ouija board.
February 19, 1990

How can the government ignore the fact that the deepest nets and the largest nets used in the Atlantic Ocean are the nets of the over 100 foreign trawlers licensed by this government, not the 60 Canadian trawlers in our offshore fleet, and that if the spawning grounds are disrupted, a codfish will not spawn.
How would the minister like it if he had a Soviet trawler barging through his bedroom? Cancel the licences.
Oh, oh!

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is obviously a great expert on spawning, although I do not know how much he knows about bedrooms.
The hon. member is well known to spawn a great deal of subterfuge in these matters, but I should point out again that foreign vessels fishing for under-utilized or surplus stocks, which Canadian fishermen are not interested in harvesting, do not fish where cod are spawning. That is why their incidental catch of cod is minuscule, small enough to be barely measurable.
Once again the hon. member is floating a red herring in this House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment. The minister knows that around 14 million tires are now on fire in my riding, and I, along with close to 1,000 of my neighbours, have been evacuated from our homes.
Unless something is done, experts say that the fire could bum for some time releasing toxins into the air and water. People in my riding want to know what resources this government has available to extinguish the fire and monitor the health and safety effects. When will this government appoint a minister responsible for this?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although this fire is a provincial responsibility, this government has provided the Ontario government with information to help with the monitoring of the smoke fumes and to assist local firefighting on the Hagersville scene.
Oral Questions
I informed the House on Friday morning that we had received a request that same morning from the Ontario government to help in the analysis of air quality. A few hours later that same day, at about 3.30 in the afternoon, the Ontario environment on-scene commander called back to advise that Environment Canada assistance was not immediately required. So we did not dispatch the team and the equipment.
This morning, I phoned Minister Jim Bradley to inquire about this. He told me that we could send our team and equipment. I also extended to him, on behalf of the Government of Canada, an offer of assistance in terms of all the resources we have, such as equipment. The army is standing ready to go there, if necessary, and we are waiting for an indication of any specific requests that Ontario might have.
I would say to the minister that he is about a week late in doing this.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Didn't you hear the answer?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Try Jim Bradley.
You are not a good member asking a question a week later.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member will put his question.

I will tell the member that I have been on the scene since day one of this disaster. I have been monitoring it from there. Where has the Government of Canada been?
My supplementary question is for the Minister of National Defence, the minister responsible for Emergency Preparedness Canada. He is aware that one of the functions of Emergency Preparedness Canada, and I quote from the act, is: "To monitor any potential, imminent or actual civil emergency and to report to the minister on the emergency and any measures necessary for dealing with that emergency".
I contacted Emergency Preparedness Canada today. They told me that, yes, they were monitoring the situation through the media, and that Emergency Preparedness Canada is not on site.
Is the minister prepared to fulfil his mandate and the government's mandate to get Emergency Preparedness Canada down there to monitor the situation and to

Oral Questions
determine what steps, if necessary, the federal government can take in that area.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
My colleague, the Minister of the Environment, provided the hon. member with a short lesson in the Constitution of Canada. The Government of Ontario, through Emergency Measures Ontario, must request assistance. We have been standing by waiting for that request.
I would like the hon. member to understand that not only was there some confusion by the Government of Ontario in requesting assistance last Friday and then withdrawing the request, but to this point there has not been a request for assistance from the Government of Ontario, either to Emergency Preparedness Canada or the Department of National Defence. Both of the departments under my responsibility and the full resources of the Government of Canada are available. We wish to help, and when requested we will respond as rapidly and as efficiently as possible.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment. Over 1,000 people in Hagersville met yesterday to voice their need for answers, their need for urgent action. The water table is being destroyed. We have a situation where cancer causing fumes are going into the air.
Why has it taken until today for that minister to offer the use of the armed forces of this country, despite the fact that minister was asked twice last week to take immediate, urgent, fast action to deal with that situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we sympathize with the people of Hagersville, and we understand their concern in the circumstances.
That is why last week, people from my department offered their services to those who are fighting the fire. We provided information, expertise on predicting air currents.
On Friday, when we received a request from the Government of Ontario, we immediately gave an affirmative response and took steps to send staff from my department, including experts and equipment.
However, late Friday afternoon, we heard the request was cancelled. This morning, I wanted to check the situation with the Ontario Minister of the Environment. He told me-and I saw there had been some confusion about the messages sent by the Government of Ontario-that we could now send the team of technicians and the team of experts.
I also said, Mr. Speaker, that the Government of Canada was offering the Government of Ontario all its resources to fight this fire. I added that the Minister of National Defence had authorized me to offer sending in the Canadian military to fight this fir, with all the necessary equipment.
\ English]

Mr. Speaker, I think it is shameful that this government should attempt to put its responsibilities off on the Province of Ontario. It has responsibilities to this country as a national government. The minister can sit there and laugh but the people in Hagersville are not laughing.
I ask this minister who has ignored these questions so fully up to this point-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is a serious matter. I would ask the hon. member to put his question.

Where else across this country are there similar dumps? How many hundreds of large dumps of tires like this, that threaten people, exist across this country which this minister has done nothing about?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by answering the first part of the question. This government respects the Constitution and the jurisdictions of the provinces, and we cannot intervene in this case if the province of Ontario does not ask us to do so. We have done everything we could do so far, and we are now waiting for specific requests. We said that we were ready to help. National Defence would like to help. We have the army. We have the equipment. We have what is necessary. We want to go, Mr. Speaker, but we are not going to invade Ontario with Canadian troops.
Second, we have made an inventory of federal dump sites, and we know that as far as federal sites are concerned, there are no dangerous stockpiles. Tomorrow, in Toronto, we will have a meeting of Deputy
February 19, 1990

Environment Ministers from across Canada, and we will establish a set of conditions for stockpiling this kind of material.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General of Canada. My question is: Can the minister tell us today whether the RCMP is now investigating a certain Kenneth Ford of Costa Rica who cheated the Canadian Government of $6 million and whether it is investigating other individuals and/or groups who defrauded the Canadian Government through this tax program the Liberals had in 1983?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment. All week Canadians have watched the burning of 15 acres of tires. These 14 million burning tires will produce 42 million litres of toxic oil run-off. What has been collected to date represents only one-half of 1 per cent of the potential oil run-off. If the oil toxins enter the groundwater it will contaminate the drinking water for both people and livestock. This is a major environmental catastrophe.
When will the federal government act and not wait on the province. I have felt for years that this law should be changed.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It's the law. It's your law.
Oral Questions
Well then we should change it, sir. Are there any federal plans to aid this area?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Environment does not have the power to change the Constitution of the country. We must respect the Constitution. This is the truth, it must be said.
Although this is a provincial responsibility, we have been very active monitoring the situation, sending people down there, and providing the Ontario Minister of the Environment with information on weather forecasts. We have also said that we would like to be invited to step in with resources, with the army.
On Friday morning we received a request. We immediately took measures to dispatch people and equipment, but a few hours later we received a cancellation of that request. This morning I checked with the minister himself as to why this was happening and he told me that we could send in our specialists. I also added that the Government of Canada would be very happy to be there. I offered him the full assistance of the federal government in terms of equipment, troops, people and everything. We stand ready to help.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same Minister. A renowned chemical engineer at Laval University has called the tire fire a more serious environmental threat than the 1988 PCB warehouse fire in Saint-Basile-le-Grand, Quebec, because of its potential to bum for months.
What are the federal plans to deal with the long-term effects after the fire is over while we have not acted with the province?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a most relevant question. We have not waited for a disaster to act. We have implemented research projects across Canada to develop new recycling processes for used tires. These research projects have resulted in the construction of about six new recycling facilities either being built or in operation.
However, it is not enough. We must do more than that. At the level of the federal and provincial Departments of Environment, there will be a meeting tomorrow of deputy ministers concerning this question. We are

February 19, 1990
Oral Questions
considering new requirements for the proper and safe storage of used tires in Canada.
In this case in Hagersville, the provincial government knew that this was dangerous and it issued instructions to ask the owner to change the storage and distribute the tires into smaller piles. The owner decided to challenge this direction in court and this case is pending now. That is the reason for this huge pile of tires. The hon. member is right, we must make sure it does not happen again in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. We learned this morning that the Department of National Health and Welfare waited nine days before notifying the Canadian public that carcinogenic substances had been found in a dozen brands of fruit juice, including Bright's, Martins, A&P, Dominion, IGA, Food City, Cavalier, Timothy's, Calbeck's, Pantry Shelf, Sunshine and Libby's Pineapple Juice.
Canadians of all ages drink these juices. These juices are part of the basic diet of young infants.
Mr. Speaker, why did the minister risk the lives of Canadians by waiting for nine days before notifying consumers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, precisely because we care about the health of Canadians, we conducted a serious investigation and waited for the results. The company removed its product and a press release was issued to that effect.

Mr. Speaker, I see several Conservative members smiling, but this is an extremely serious subject and I wonder if they gave this juice to their children.

Does the minister realize, and is he conscious that these reconstituted juices contain 40 times the acceptable level of cancer-causing chemicals?
This morning an article in The Ottawa Sun states: "Health and Welfare Canada and Sun D'Or both knew about the contamination when production was halted on February 7 but it was not announced to the public until last February 16".
Furthermore, the Health Protection Branch did not believe that the risk was great enough for a public announcement, said a Health and Welfare spokesman. "We reserve the public announcement for when a situation is life-threatening."
I would like to ask the minister, is this how the ministry addresses food consumption? Is this their response to consumers, senior citizens, young children and babies? Is this a sense of responsibility, waiting nine days, knowing that a product contained cancer-causing agents?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the hon. member has put his
question.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, again, we are concerned about the quality of life of Canadians and about consumers having a quality product, and that is why we shall continue to monitor the quality of this product. We intend to ensure that existing measures can remedy the situation and that this will never happen again. Before a press release could be issued, a serious study was necessary to prove the product could have serious consequences. The company has acted responsibly, the product has been withdrawn, and we shall continue to monitor the quality of this product very carefully.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of the Environment on another issue where he seems to be completely out of touch with his provincial colleagues.
On December 21, Cameco Limited pleaded guilty to two charges under the Atomic Energy Control Act for dumping 440,000 gallons of contaminated mine water into Wollaston Lake. They were given the maximum penalty under that act, $5,000 each, which is half of what you get for smoking on Parliament Hill.
February 19, 1990

On February 8 the Government of Saskatchewan brought charges for which the maximum fine is $1 million. Now Cameco is challenging the Saskatchewan charges in court saying they do not have jurisdiction over the uranium mining industry.
Will the minister support the charges being brought by the Saskatchewan government, will he bring in his own charges, or will he finally agree to an inquiry to straighten out the mess that the uranium mining industry in this country is in?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows that the AECB examined the situation of Cameco. He also knows the AECB laid charges. He also knows that there were fines levied.
In respect to his specific question relating to a challenge in the courts, it is before the courts and that is where it will stay.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the Minister of the Environment. The Minister of the Environment has not shown that he even knows that an issue exists at Wollaston Lake. We have not heard at all whether he supports an inquiry into that situation where there are issues pertaining not only to the environment but to benefits to the local community and to the whole future of the uranium mining industry and how it relates to local communities.
Is the minister going to take action? Is he going to take a close look at what is happening, or is he going to be caught out to lunch on a Saskatchewan environment issue again like he was on Rafferty-Alameda?

The Minister of the Environment, his officials and officials of AECB have been in contact on this issue.
The hon. member and all viewers should understand that there is a regulatory process and it was that regulatoiy process which investigated and laid charges for which fines were paid. If there is a legal challenge in the courts, I think hon. members and you, Mr. Speaker, know that there is a right to follow the judicial course of action. The case is there and I do not think I can make any comments about it.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. On Friday of last week I was asking about the worsening crisis situation in Ethiopia. The minister responded by mentioning that at least one ship had been diverted to Port Sudan. The minister will know that last week his colleague, the Minister for External Relations, referred to the threatened famine situation because of the deterioration in Ethiopia to at least two million people.
In view of the fact that the government of Ethiopia had agreed to some safe corridors that could be manned by the churches for the distribution of relief, and those safe corridors are now totally unusable because of increased rebel activity, can the minister assure us of two things? First of all, since we do provide assistance to all sides, that we can use our efforts to try to open up those international relief corridors again. They are essential to saving the lives of at least two million people.
Second, since former Presidents Jimmy Carter and Julius Nyerere have been chairing some peace negotiations, will the minister contact in particular former

February 19, 1990
Point of Order
President Carter to see if we can have some acceleration of those peace talks? Without peace there can never be a hope of overcoming the famine situation in Ethiopia.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a tragedy that is getting worse for reasons to which the hon. member has referred. We are working with the United Nations, with other countries that are involved and with NGOs to try to open corridors that can stay open to try to bring relief to trapped people. We are also seeking to identify alternative routes. I think the realistic conclusion is that unless there is a ceasefire or some agreements to suspend hostilities, all of this will be in vain. We are nonetheless working vigorously with others who are concerned to try to achieve some means of getting food to entrapped people.
I have signed a letter today to former President Carter offering Canada's full and continuing support and, indeed, suggesting some actions that might be helpful for us to take if the peace negotiation succeeds in the hope that perhaps the prospect of that action may strengthen the hand of former President Carter and President Nyerere.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. I have just returned from Clyde River in my constituency where I bought some groceries. A dozen apples cost over $8, a dozen eggs cost $5, a five-pound bag of potatoes cost over $9 and the average income is $10,000.
The Minister of Finance wants to limit that northern purchasing power by putting a 7 per cent goods and services tax on almost everything my constituents need for good nutritional value. How can the minister-
Not eggs.
The hon. member says "not eggs".

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member and others would allow the hon. member who has been given the floor the right to ask the question, keeping in mind the time, the minister could respond.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I must advise members that when you limit the purchasing power for
other goods, people will not be able to buy as many groceries. I should inform the hon. member.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance to justify his claim that the north will be better off with the goods and services tax. Where are the studies he said in October he had to back up his claim? Will the minister reassure northern parents and families by recognizing the higher cost of living and exempting northerners who are already paying $4.29 for one litre of milk from this unfair tax?
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member would like to acknowledge to the House that apples, eggs and potatoes are not subject to the GST.
Transportation is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member over here said that transportation is subject to the GST. That is wrong. Any tax on transportation is credited out so that there is no tax on transportation as part of the cost of food.
I think it is very important for the hon. member to understand that. I think that all in this House understand the level of the price of food and other commodities in the north but that looks at only one part of the impact of the GST. The GST is very positive for the industries of the north, particularly the mining and the oil and gas industries. Those industries will receive credits on all the taxes they pay. It will make them more competitive. It will allow for mines that might otherwise be closed to stay open for a longer period of time and that will provide employment. That will provide the wherewithal for northerners to pay for the goods that my colleague has referred to. So I caution him not to be too narrow in his analysis of the impact of the GST.

I say that the time has surely come when this House must speak in a firm, solid and unified way by saying enough is enough. Interest rates in this country are now much too high. Interest rates are hurting the ordinary Canadian citizen and it is about time we brought them down and brought them down now.
I appeal to the government back-benchers. I appeal to the government ministers across the way that they take the lead from the finance committee and say to the Minister of Finance, with a budget coming down tomorrow, that the bank rate in this country is much too high and it is hurting ordinary Canadian citizens.
In the last three weeks we have seen a jump in the bank rate in this country of one full per centage point. I suggest that the interest rates in this country now are out of control. The Bank of Canada has lost any meaningful control it had on monetary policy in the country. Instead, monetary policy is now being controlled by the international investors and exchange markets around the world.
Going back a few weeks to January 18, the Bank of Canada dropped the interest rate by 29 basis points. It
went down to 12.14 per cent. A lot of people were optimistic, saying that the bank rate in this country would be going down. Perhaps it was a signal of positive things to come in the economy and perhaps we were getting back to a more sane monetary policy once again.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this debate today on the subject of interest rates here in Canada, especially on the report to the House by the Finance Committee on April 14, 1989.

The important point to make first is that the report we are discussing is not an opposition report. It is not a report of the Liberal Party or the New Democratic Party. It is a report of the finance committee of the House of Commons. Not only that, it is an unanimous report.
With all due respect to some members opposite who have made some very critical remarks about the recommendation that this report be adopted, I suggest to them that what they have first and foremost on their hands is a problem to be resolved within their own caucus. I suggest to them that if they are unwilling to support this recommendation, if the Minister of Finance is content to toss it aside, why do they not remove all their members from the finance committee?
Why not see if they can find within their caucus as honest a man as the current chairman and replace him with somebody who will follow their line on interest rates? This is an all-party, unanimous report of the finance committee of the House of Commons, recommending that monetary policy in Canada be relaxed and that the rate of interest be reduced.
It is very interesting. I was refreshing my memory by looking at the report a few moments ago. It comments in the introduction that at the time of writing the bank rate was nearly 400 basis points above rates prevailing in early 1988 and at its highest level in five years. In the introductory paragraph it also observes: "The surge in interest rates was particularly sharp in the four-month period between end of November 1988 to the end of March, 1989, when rates jumped nearly two full per centage points".
If I am not mistaken we had a general election in this country on November 21, 1988. Does it not strike one as being somewhat odd that starting the end of November 1988, just after the general election, until the end of March, 1989, rates jumped that high, that sharply? I suppose it could be argued that right after the election Canadians went on a spending binge and a credit binge and that all of a sudden the Governor of the Bank of Canada discovered there was rampaging inflation and
February 19, 1990

that "we had better wrestle it to the ground and we had better do it right now".
It strikes me as being just a little odd that none of this was foreseeable during those weeks of campaigning across the country when the Minister of Finance was happy to tell everyone that things were just great. Then, as soon as the election had been won, interest rates surged upward. That was not the end of the surge. They have continued to surge from 8.63 per cent in January, 1988, to a little over 12.5 per cent when this report of the finance committee was issued. On February 15 they were at 13.32 per cent.
Another aspect that is very concerning to all of us is the difference between the Canadian rate and the U.S. rate. In April when the finance committee issued its report and was concerned we had a spread of 2.75 per cent. It expressed its concern that it was historically very high. As I stand here today, we are looking at a spread of over 5 per cent between Canadian and U.S. rates.

encourage people to go out and invest and do new things. The policies of this government are not intended to help small business. The policies of this government are not intended to encourage research and development.
This government has two policy objectives in the economic sphere: first, it is fixated on the deficit and thinks it wants to reduce it or says it wants to reduce it. Second, its monetary policy demonstrates that it has a fixation on inflation and it wants to eliminate it.
I do not think anyone would quarrel with the idea that we should have lower deficits. We do not want inflation, but I think it is legitimate to ask whether or not there are some other policy objectives the Government of Canada ought to make priority in dealing with the important economic problems facing us.
Why is it that the government has decided inflation should eliminate concerns about employment from the economic agenda? Why is it that the deficit has taken control of all aspects of government policy? At a time when we need economic growth in Canada, when we need to address the problems that we have in regions like the Atlantic, the prairies, the north, and at times when we have to deal with high unemployment, sometimes we have to readjust the economic priorities as we see them.
We have had some seven years of sustained economic growth which began in 1982. We have a government that was twice elected to reduce the deficit. By the time of the next election, three-quarters of the national debt will have been accumulated by government elected on a mandate of reducing the deficit.
When we look at the financial statements the government will present to us tomorrow, we know roughly what the figures are going to be. We see the problem in the annual deficit is not so much the level of the debt. Although it is huge and it is a problem, the difficulty is in the level of interest rates.
The biggest borrower in Canada, the entity that is absorbing so much of the debt, is the Government of Canada. As we raise these interest rates a point here and a point there, from 8.63 per cent in January, 1988, to more than 13.25 per cent now, we see the deficit gets out of control. Not only that, these monetary policies are going to cause a major recession in Canada with the result being higher unemployment, greater demand on
